findings.title: Unauthenticated analytics debug endpoint exposes raw event data
findings.description: /api/analytics/debug has zero authentication. Any anonymous HTTP GET returns raw analytics_events rows including session_ids, event types, room_ids, and real user data. All sibling analytics endpoints (metrics, referrals, proxy-metrics) correctly check ANALYTICS_ADMIN_TOKEN or cookie. This one does not.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker GETs https://gamesnight.ng/api/analytics/debug. 2. Receives JSON with last 10 raw analytics_events and event type counts. 3. Extracts session_ids — real user identifiers — and room_ids. 4. Uses session_ids to query /api/stats/[sessionId] for game history of any user.
findings.impact: Exposure of real user session IDs, game activity patterns, room codes. Enables targeted enumeration of any player's game history.
findings.recommendation: Add the same auth check used in proxy-metrics.ts: check ANALYTICS_ADMIN_TOKEN cookie before serving. Or delete the endpoint entirely — it's a debug tool that should never be in production.

findings.title: Profile write auth bypassed on first write (token bootstrap race)
findings.description: PUT /api/profile/[sessionId] checks X-Session-Token against the stored session_token. But if no row exists yet (new player), existing.session_token is null — so the check `if (existing?.session_token && existing.session_token !== providedToken)` always passes. Any caller that sends ANY non-empty token string can create or overwrite a profile with any sessionId on the first write. The attacker supplies a UUID of their choosing as both the sessionId path param and X-Session-Token, and they own that profile permanently.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker picks a victim's session_id (obtainable from /api/analytics/debug or by watching leaderboard data). 2. Sends PUT /api/profile/<victim_session_id> with X-Session-Token: <any-uuid>. 3. If victim has no profile row yet, the write succeeds. 4. Attacker now controls victim's profile — can set display_name, whatsapp, email, referred_by. 5. Attacker's token is persisted. Victim's legitimate write is rejected as 403.
findings.impact: Profile takeover for any user who hasn't yet written their profile. Attacker can associate a phone/email they control with another user's session, stealing referral attribution and corrupting contact data.
findings.recommendation: On first write (no existing row), the server should generate the session_token server-side, not accept it from the caller. Return it in a Set-Cookie or response body for the legitimate client to store. Never trust a caller-supplied token as an ownership proof on creation.

findings.title: Weak analytics password in .env.local (@Geraldwan1)
findings.description: ANALYTICS_PASSWORD=@Geraldwan1. This is a personal password with predictable structure: name + number + symbol. ANALYTICS_ADMIN_TOKEN='your-secret-token-here' — the token is still the placeholder value, meaning the analytics dashboard is protected only by the username/password, and the token check in /api/analytics/metrics accepts this placeholder.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker targets /api/analytics/auth with credential stuffing or targeted guessing. 2. Username 'admin' + common password patterns (name+number combos) succeeds. 3. Auth endpoint sets analytics_session cookie = 'your-secret-token-here'. 4. Attacker now accesses all analytics: game plays, player counts, share data, referral chains, player contact info. 5. /api/analytics/metrics accepts X-Admin-Token: your-secret-token-here directly, no login needed.
findings.impact: Full analytics dashboard access. Exposure of all player session data, referral relationships, contact info, virality metrics. Also: the default ANALYTICS_ADMIN_TOKEN means any attacker who knows the placeholder value (it's public in .env.example) can hit /api/analytics/metrics directly without the password.
findings.recommendation: 1. Change ANALYTICS_PASSWORD to a random 20+ char string. 2. Generate a real ANALYTICS_ADMIN_TOKEN: run `openssl rand -hex 32` and set it. 3. The .env.example already documents this — just do it.

findings.title: Next.js CSRF bypass via null origin (GHSA-mq59-m269-xvcx)
findings.description: Running next@16.2.4. GHSA-mq59-m269-xvcx affects Next.js <16.1.7: a null origin header bypasses Server Actions CSRF protections. This app uses Next.js API routes (pages/api/), not Server Actions, so the direct attack surface is limited. However the project is on a version with known CSRF issues and other moderate CVEs (HTTP request smuggling in rewrites: GHSA-ggv3-7p47-pfv8).
findings.exploit_scenario: For Server Actions (not used here): attacker sends a cross-origin form POST with Origin: null. Next.js 16.x < 16.1.7 treats null as same-origin and processes the action. Not directly exploitable with current pages/api/ architecture, but the version should still be patched.
findings.impact: MEDIUM — current architecture doesn't use Server Actions. Risk is latent; if Server Actions are adopted without patching, CSRF is trivially exploitable.
findings.recommendation: Run `npm install next@latest` or pin to next@16.1.7+. The audit flags multiple moderate CVEs in the installed version. This is a straightforward package update.

findings.title: Supabase project URL and ref hardcoded in setup-db.mjs
findings.description: SUPABASE_URL and PROJECT_REF are hardcoded literals in the script. The SERVICE_KEY is correctly read from env. But hardcoding the project URL means any future project migration requires a code change (not just env var update), and the project reference is permanently embedded in git history. Low severity on its own but combined with Finding #3, the Supabase project is fully enumerable.
findings.exploit_scenario: Not directly exploitable on its own. Combined with a leaked service role key, the hardcoded URL removes one barrier to exploitation.
findings.impact: Low — the anon key (public by design) is already in NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL. This just confirms the project ref in git history.
findings.recommendation: Move SUPABASE_URL to an env var: `const SUPABASE_URL = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`. Already set in env files — just reference it.

findings.title: No rate limiting on any API endpoint
findings.description: Zero rate limiting across all 25 API endpoints. The analytics/auth endpoint accepts unlimited login attempts. The rooms/create endpoint can be called in a tight loop to generate thousands of room codes. The profile/resolve endpoint can be used to enumerate registered emails.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker scripts POST /api/analytics/auth in a loop with password wordlists. 2. No lockout, no rate limit, no CAPTCHA — pure brute force. With password '@Geraldwan1' (name+number pattern), targeted guessing succeeds quickly. Also: POST /api/rooms/check?code=XXXXXX can enumerate room codes at network speed.
findings.impact: Credential brute force on analytics admin. Room code enumeration. Email enumeration via /api/profile/resolve (200 = exists, 404 = doesn't).
findings.recommendation: Add rate limiting at the middleware layer. For Next.js: use `next-rate-limit` or implement via Vercel Edge middleware. Priority: auth endpoint first (max 5 attempts/minute/IP), then content endpoints.

findings.title: No Content Security Policy headers
findings.description: next.config.ts has no security headers configured. No CSP, no X-Frame-Options, no X-Content-Type-Options. The app injects Google Tag Manager via dangerouslySetInnerHTML — this is a legitimate use but without CSP, any XSS vulnerability (future) has no secondary mitigation.
findings.exploit_scenario: If an XSS were introduced (e.g., via player names rendered without escaping in a future feature), no CSP would prevent exfiltration of session storage, localStorage (session_id, session_token), or analytics cookies.
findings.impact: Defense-in-depth gap. No direct exploit currently — but no safety net either.
findings.recommendation: Add security headers in next.config.ts via the `headers()` async function: X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin. CSP is more complex due to GTM but start with the simpler headers.

findings.title: IDOR on /api/stats/[sessionId] — any session's game history is readable
findings.description: GET /api/stats/[sessionId] returns full game history for any sessionId with no auth. sessionIds are obtainable from the debug endpoint (Finding #1) or the leaderboard. There is no check that the requester owns the sessionId they're querying.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. From /api/analytics/debug, extract session_ids from analytics_events. 2. GET /api/stats/<any_session_id>. 3. Receive full game history: which games played, scores, results, timestamps.
findings.impact: Behavioral data exposure for all users. Not financial, but privacy relevant — reveals play patterns, frequency, performance.
findings.recommendation: Either: (a) require X-Session-Token match (same pattern as profile PUT), or (b) treat stats as public by design (the leaderboard is already public) and document this as intentional. Currently it's an unintentional IDOR.
